questions.q: What are the two ways a model change breaks vector search, and which one is silent?
options: Schema drift (loud) and data drift (loud)
Both failures always raise errors
API timeout (loud) and API rate limiting (quiet)

Dimension mismatch is the loud one — SQL Server's VECTOR(1536) throws a hard error on a 1,024-d insert — while semantic drift is the quiet one: same dimension, different geometry, retrieval degrades with no error
questions.explain: Dimension mismatch fails loud — VECTOR(1536) rejects a 1024-d insert with a hard error. Semantic drift fails silent: same dimension, different geometry, plausible-looking distances, and degrading retrieval quality with no error.

questions.q: What does the chapter say about padding or truncating vectors to force a dimension fit?
options: Zero-pad 1024-d vectors into a 1536-d column — it is the recommended migration shortcut
Truncate to the smaller dimension — distance math still works
Never pad or truncate vectors to force a dimension fit — zero-padding produces vectors that compare meaninglessly against true vectors; dimension is identity
Padding is fine as long as you also update the DiskANN index
questions.explain: Never pad or truncate to force a dimension fit: a zero-padded 1024-d vector compares meaninglessly against true 1536-d vectors — dimension is identity, and mismatched vectors are silent corruption.

questions.q: What is the zero-downtime migration pattern for an embedding model change?
options: Side-by-side: add a second vector column, backfill it with the new model, build a second DiskANN index, eval-gate the cutover, then retire the old column — retrieval never stops serving
Copy rows from the old model into the new column without re-embedding
Run the migration in a single transaction
Drop the vector index, alter the column type, re-embed everything, rebuild — during a maintenance window
questions.explain: The zero-downtime pattern is side-by-side: new column, throttled resumable backfill, second DiskANN index, eval-gated flag flip, old column retained as rollback — retrieval never stops serving.

questions.q: Why must the retrieval procedure be model-aware from day one?
options: Because the optimizer needs the model name for its cost estimates
A @modelVersion parameter selecting the column and the ModelName predicate turns migrations into flag flips instead of code deploys — and rollbacks get faster exactly when you need them fast
Because DiskANN requires the model name at index build time
It is only needed for auditing
questions.explain: A model-aware retrieval procedure with a @modelVersion parameter turns migrations into flag flips instead of code deploys, making rollbacks fast when they matter most.

questions.q: How should vendor model deprecations and version pinning be handled?
options: Ignore deprecation notices until the endpoint stops responding
Pin only the major version and let the vendor choose the rest
Use floating model aliases so upgrades happen automatically

Pin exact model versions in configuration (model name plus version date or snapshot ID) and treat vendor deprecation notices like certificate expirations — with deadlines, a registry, and scheduled migrations
questions.explain: Pin exact model versions — text-embedding-3-small may resolve to a different snapshot tomorrow — record retirement dates in a registry, and treat deprecation notices like certificate expirations with a scheduled migration plan.
